principles.name: Respect the Individual
principles.description: Listen to each other, show empathy, celebrate differences, and know that great ideas can come from anywhere; build teams where associates feel supported and can grow.
evidence_signals: Sought out and used an idea from a junior colleague, a store associate or another team
Handled a disagreement by listening first and shows empathy for the other side
Mentored or developed teammates with a visible result
Treats front-line users (store associates, drivers, pickers) as people whose time matters

principles.name: Act with Integrity
principles.description: Do the right thing; be honest, fair and transparent; do what you say you will do and earn trust.
evidence_signals: Raised a bad-news issue (risk, defect, missed date) early and openly
Kept a commitment or explicitly reset it instead of letting it slip silently
Chose the compliant or fair option when a shortcut was available, and explains the cost
Credits others accurately and owns own mistakes

principles.name: Serve Our Customers and Members
principles.description: Work every day to improve the experience of customers, Sam's Club members and the associates who serve them, aiming to exceed their expectations and help them save money and live better.
evidence_signals: Names a concrete customer, member or associate pain and how it was measured
Ties a technical or product decision to price, availability, convenience or trust for the customer
Weighs cost to serve so savings can be passed on (everyday low cost supports everyday low price)
Checked the result for the customer after launch

principles.name: Strive for Excellence
principles.description: Move with speed, pay attention to detail, and hold high expectations of yourself and those you work with; keep improving and innovating.
evidence_signals: Delivered quickly while protecting quality on what mattered, for example a peak-season readiness plan
Caught a detail others missed (data error, edge case, capacity gap) and fixed the root cause
Improved a process or system with a measured gain in speed, reliability or cost
Raised the bar for the team with a mechanism such as tests, load tests or reviews

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, interest in retail tech, logistics, sometimes light technical questions. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: One or two medium-to-hard data structures problems, sometimes SQL. Reported as 60 to 90 minutes. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding round
rounds.notes: Live coding plus questions on resume projects and core fundamentals (Java, concurrency, Spring Boot are often reported). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Design round
rounds.notes: Low-level object design for earlier levels; high-level distributed design at retail scale (inventory, order management, checkout under burst, pickup, pricing) for senior and above. Often includes a deep dive on a past system.

rounds.name: Hiring manager round
rounds.notes: Conversational but behavioral in substance; STAR answers expected on ownership, conflict, scale and why Walmart. Some light technical discussion.

rounds.name: Behavioral and values discussion
rounds.notes: Often folded into the hiring manager round rather than a separate interview; probes collaboration, mistakes and the four Walmart values.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, eligibility and motivation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Experience, culture fit and behavioral questions.

rounds.name: Product sense and case
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior product manager or product leader
rounds.notes: Product design and metrics questions on Walmart products; some teams give a case or take-home a few days ahead and ask for a presentation.

rounds.name: Leadership and collaboration
rounds.notes: Leading projects, working with engineering and business partners, failures and trade-offs.

rounds.name: Director interview
rounds.notes: Optional final round reported for some roles; strategic case discussion.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: SQL and Python, sometimes an ML problem such as time-series forecasting. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Statistics and ML fundamentals
rounds.notes: Regression, classification, overfitting, model evaluation, experimentation; reported as several 30 to 45 minute rounds.

rounds.name: ML case study
rounds.notes: A business problem (forecasting, pricing, fraud, search) judged on framing, data pipeline, model choice and evaluation.

rounds.name: Hiring manager and behavioral
rounds.notes: Past projects, conflict, stress and why Walmart.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate improved something for an end customer or a front-line user and how they knew it worked
A mistake the candidate made, how they surfaced it, and what changed afterwards
A disagreement with a partner team, product or business stakeholder and how it was resolved

question_patterns.theme: Speed with quality under peak pressure
question_patterns.pattern: Delivering against a fixed, high-stakes date (a holiday peak, a launch) without letting quality slip
A time priorities, requirements or the organization changed suddenly and how the candidate adjusted
Mentoring, onboarding or growing a teammate, or including a quieter voice in a decision
Walk through a system or product the candidate built that runs at large scale, their own role, and the hardest technical challenge
A critical technical or product decision made without full data and how risk was managed
Motivation for Walmart Global Tech specifically and how the candidate's goals fit the team
Design inventory, order management or fulfillment routing across stores, warehouses, pickup and delivery, with consistency and reconciliation trade-offs
Design or harden a customer-facing flow (cart, checkout, search) for a known traffic spike many times the baseline
Design a system that runs in thousands of stores with unreliable connectivity, such as sensors, pickup scheduling or associate tools

question_patterns.theme: ML fundamentals in a retail setting
question_patterns.pattern: Explain a model choice, evaluation method or failure mode (overfitting, bias, drift) for a retail problem such as forecasting or fraud
Improve a Walmart digital product (app, pickup and delivery, Walmart+) for a chosen customer segment and define success metrics
Choose success metrics for a feature, or explain how a feature moves a given metric

question_patterns.theme: Cost to serve and low prices
question_patterns.pattern: Weigh customer value against operating cost for a fulfillment, pricing or membership decision, consistent with everyday low cost and everyday low price

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work. What happened next?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real mistake with real consequences. Explain how the candidate noticed it, how quickly and openly they told the people affected, and what they did to limit the damage. Then show the root cause and the lasting change (a test, a checklist, a review step) with evidence it worked. Walmart interviewers listen for honesty and follow-through rather than a perfect record. Pitfalls: a disguised strength, blaming others, or no change afterwards.

sample_questions.question: How do you handle challenges or disagreements with cross-functional teams?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use a specific story, not a general philosophy. Describe the partner team and what each side wanted. Show the candidate listening to understand the other side's constraints, using data to frame options, and agreeing on a decision and an owner. Close with the outcome and how the relationship held up. Strong answers mention respect for the other team's goals. Pitfalls: winning by escalation, or a conflict with no real stakes.

sample_questions.question: Describe a project you spearheaded from start to finish.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the goal and why it mattered to customers or the business. Show what the candidate personally drove: framing the problem, getting buy-in, planning, and unblocking the team. Name one hard moment and how it was handled. Quantify the result and what was learned. At senior levels show influence across teams. Pitfalls: 'we' with no clear personal role, or a project with no measurable outcome.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you successfully handled a challenging customer issue.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the customer (external or internal) and the issue in concrete terms. Show the candidate taking ownership, finding the real cause rather than the symptom, and keeping the customer informed. Describe the fix and a step that stopped it happening again for other customers. Quantify the result where possible. Pitfalls: a story where the customer was simply wrong, or a fix that only helped one person.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to adapt to a significant change.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the change (reorg, new priority, new technology) and its impact on the candidate's work. Show how they re-planned quickly, kept the team informed, and protected the most important commitments. Mention what they let go of and why. Close with the result and what they would repeat. Pitfalls: complaining about the change, or simply waiting for direction.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about something you built at large scale and the main technical challenges you faced.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give scale in numbers (requests, data volume, stores, users). Explain the architecture briefly, then the hardest problem (consistency, latency, peak load, migration) and the options considered. Be clear about the candidate's own decisions versus the team's. Close with results, an incident or lesson, and what they would change today. Pitfalls: listing technologies without trade-offs, or no clear personal contribution.

sample_questions.question: Describe a critical technical decision you had to make with incomplete information.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain what was unknown and why waiting was costly. Show how the candidate gathered the best available evidence, judged whether the decision was reversible, and reduced risk (feature flag, staged rollout, fallback). Say who they consulted and how they communicated the uncertainty honestly. Close with how it turned out and what they learned. Pitfalls: claiming certainty, or never revisiting the decision.

sample_questions.question: Why Walmart Global Tech rather than another tech company?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connect the candidate's interests to what is distinctive about Walmart: physical and digital commerce at huge scale, problems where software touches stores, supply chain and millions of customers, and a mission of saving people money. Mention a specific team area or public engineering topic. Tie it to the candidate's career goals. Pitfalls: generic praise, or only compensation and stability.

sample_questions.question: How do you prioritize between two conflicting product requests?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out a clear method: the goal both requests serve, the impact on customers and the business, cost and effort, urgency, and reversibility. Show how the candidate would get data, involve the requesters, decide, and explain the trade-off openly. Mention what happens to the lower-priority request. Pitfalls: trying to do both, or deciding by who is most senior.

sample_questions.question: Design a real-time inventory system for about 10,000 stores plus the online site.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale (stores times SKUs), update sources (POS sales, receiving, returns, online orders) and freshness needs. Propose event-driven updates per store into a central availability service, with reservations for online and pickup orders. Discuss that store counts are physically uncertain, so promise from a buffered number and reconcile with scans. Cover partitioning by store, idempotent events, offline stores, and strong consistency at reservation versus eventual consistency for browse. Pitfalls: one global lock or ignoring shrink.

sample_questions.question: Design cart and checkout so it survives Black Friday traffic many times the normal peak.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Estimate peak load and the hot items. Pre-scale for the known date and load test. Keep browse cacheable and checkout strongly consistent. Use a queue or waiting room with honest position updates, inventory reservations with timeouts for hot items, idempotent payment calls, and graceful degradation (turn off recommendations before checkout). Discuss monitoring, rollback and a game-day plan. Pitfalls: assuming autoscaling alone handles a doorbuster spike, or overselling.

sample_questions.question: Design an online-order, pick-up-in-store (curbside) system.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the flow: order, slot booking, store picking, staging, customer arrival and handoff. Model slot capacity from associate labor and parking spots, not only from inventory. Handle substitutions when an item is missing, real-time arrival check-in, and associate devices that must work with poor store Wi-Fi. Discuss notifications, failure modes and metrics such as wait time and order accuracy. Pitfalls: ignoring the associate's workflow or store capacity.

sample_questions.question: Design a pricing system that recommends prices and lets merchants approve changes.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Separate price recommendation (models using demand, competitor and cost data) from price publication. Add business rules and guardrails (floors, price-match rules, legal limits), an approval workflow, and an audit trail. Explain how prices reach the site and thousands of store shelves consistently, with effective dates and rollback. Keep EDLP in mind: stable prices matter more than constant swings. Pitfalls: letting a model publish prices with no controls.

sample_questions.question: How would you detect and reduce overfitting or bias in a classifier?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define overfitting as a gap between training and validation performance. Cover proper splits (time-based for retail data), cross-validation, regularization, simpler models, more data and early stopping. For bias, check performance by segment, look at label and sampling bias, and pick fairness or calibration metrics that fit the use case. Mention monitoring for drift after launch. Pitfalls: only listing techniques without saying how to diagnose the problem.

sample_questions.question: What do you consider when building a predictive model, for example for demand forecasting?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the business decision the forecast drives (replenishment, staffing) and its cost of error. Cover data (sales history, promotions, holidays, weather, stockouts that hide true demand), feature design, a baseline model, then candidate models. Explain evaluation over time with backtesting, the right error metric, and how forecasts are served and monitored. Pitfalls: treating sales as demand when items were out of stock.

sample_questions.question: Design a feature for the Walmart app that increases customer loyalty.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify what loyalty means (repeat purchase, Walmart+ retention, share of grocery spend). Pick a segment, for example busy families buying weekly groceries, and map their pain points. Generate options (smart reorder lists, pickup reminders, price tracking) and prioritize by impact and effort. Recommend one with a success metric, guardrails, and a test plan. Pitfalls: features with no segment, or ignoring cost to serve.

sample_questions.question: Walk me through how you would launch a new grocery pickup service.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify goals (adoption, frequency, margin) and target customers. Cover the customer journey and the store operations behind it: picking labor, staging space, slot capacity, substitutions. Propose a pilot in a few stores, launch criteria, and metrics (order accuracy, wait time, repeat rate, cost per order). Explain how to scale and what would stop the rollout. Pitfalls: treating it as only an app feature and ignoring store operations.

sample_questions.question: How would you improve walmart.com or the Walmart mobile shopping experience?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Ask for the goal and pick one customer segment. Walk through the journey (search, product page, cart, checkout, delivery) and find the biggest drop-off or pain with data. Propose two or three solutions, prioritize one, and define a primary metric (conversion, repeat purchase) and guardrails (returns, cost per order). Pitfalls: a list of features with no prioritization, or ignoring the low-price promise.

sample_questions.question: What metrics would you use to measure the success of a new product or feature?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from the feature's goal and the customer behavior it should change. Choose one primary metric, supporting metrics along the funnel, and guardrails (cost, latency, cannibalization). Explain how to set targets and measure causally with an experiment. Show how the answer changes if the metric moves the wrong way. Pitfalls: long lists with no primary metric, or vanity metrics.

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Entry level; delivers well-defined tasks and features with guidance and writes tested code.
Owns features or services within a team, handles moderate ambiguity, and starts to lead small projects and help junior engineers.
Leads complex projects and designs systems for a team, mentors others, and owns reliability for peak events.
Technical leader across several teams; shapes architecture and influences technical strategy.
Sets technical direction for an organization or platform and drives cross-org initiatives.
Owns features or a product area and its metrics with an engineering team.
Owns a product line, sets its roadmap with business partners, and drives multi-team launches.
Owns models end to end for a business problem, from framing to production monitoring, and guides junior data scientists.

persona.tone: Friendly, practical and down to earth; conversational rather than adversarial
persona.pace: Moderate; time for clarifying questions, with steady follow-ups on details
persona.pushback_style: Asks for scale and numbers, 'what was your part?', and how the design or decision holds up at peak or in a real store; brings answers back to the customer and to cost
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions about the team; no feedback given in the room

case_style.notes: Cases start from a customer segment and Walmart's physical plus digital footprint: stores, pickup and delivery, Walmart+, marketplace and associates as users. Strong answers weigh cost to serve (everyday low cost supports everyday low price) and store operations, and end with metrics. Some PM teams give the case ahead of time and ask for a presentation.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the four value names and descriptions come from corporate.walmart.com; evidence signals and weights are our estimate. Walmart also has internal Leadership Expectations built on the same values, but no official public page was found, so they are not modeled separately.

loop_structure: all round details come from third-party prep sites, not a Walmart hiring page. A separate behavioral round is not consistently reported; behavioral questions are usually inside the hiring manager round. The data_ml loop comes mainly from one prep site.

bar_by_level: level names follow Levels.fyi; internal codes (P2 to P5 and similar) are reported inconsistently across sites and are left out. Scope text is our summary. PM and data science level names come from job titles and one prep guide.
persona: no public source describes interviewer style in detail; 'conversational but behavioral in substance' is from one prep site, the rest is our inference.
scoring_weights: no public source gives competency weights; derived from the stress on customers, collaboration and retail-scale design.

sample_questions: Glassdoor pages could not be read directly; questions come from prep-site lists of candidate-reported questions. Several system design questions are illustrative examples from prep sites rather than verified candidate reports.
